usage: 결혼 is not a verb by itself; it needs 하다, and 을 marks it as the object
use 결혼식, not 결혼, for the event you physically attend with 에
축하하다 'congratulate' is the standard verb at weddings
결혼 + 생활 'life' = the ongoing state of being married, not the ceremony
examples: 저는 결혼을 했어요.
I am married. / I got married.
simple: the 했어요 (past of 하다) covers both the event and the resulting status
다음 달에 친구 결혼식에 가요.
Next month I'm going to my friend's wedding.
everyday: for attending the ceremony switch to 결혼식 + 에, never 결혼에
두 분의 결혼을 진심으로 축하드립니다.
I sincerely congratulate you both on your marriage.
real-situation: 축하드립니다 is the humble, formal congratulation you'd say or write at a wedding
nuance: 결혼 (結婚, 結 'tie/bind' + 婚 'marry') is Sino-Korean and covers two ideas at once: the act of getting married and the ongoing married state, which is why English speakers must add 하다 (결혼하다) to make it a verb — 결혼 alone is a noun. The dividing line you must learn: 결혼 is the union/marriage itself, while 결혼식 (式 'ceremony') is the wedding event you attend, so you go 결혼식에 가요, never 결혼에 가요. Compare it to 신혼 'newlywed life' and 청혼 'marriage proposal' — same 婚 root, different stages. Register is fully neutral; everyone from teens to elders uses it. The classic English-speaker pitfall is treating 결혼 like the English verb 'to marry' and producing 결혼을 만들어요 ('make a marriage') or dropping 하다 entirely; another is using 와/과 wrongly — you marry someone with ~와/과 결혼하다 (그 사람과 결혼했어요), not ~를 결혼하다.

Saying 결혼에 가요 for attending a wedding — that points at the abstract marriage, not the event; you attend the ceremony, so use 결혼식에 가요.
Marking the spouse with 를 (그 사람을 결혼했어요) — you marry WITH someone, so use ~와/과: 그 사람과 결혼했어요.

usage: 에 marks the party as the destination you head toward
열다 'open' is the most natural host verb, slightly fancier than 하다
the invitee takes 를 and the party takes 에: 친구를 파티에 초대해요
파티 is usually preceded by the occasion (생일, 송년, 환영)
examples: 오늘 파티에 가요.
I'm going to a party today.
simple: 에 with a motion verb = the place you move toward
주말에 우리 집에서 파티를 할 거예요.
I'm going to have a party at my place this weekend.
everyday: note 집에서 (에서 = where the action happens) vs 파티를 (the object you do)
송년 파티에 친구들을 모두 초대했어요.
I invited all my friends to the year-end party.
real-situation: 송년 파티 'year-end party' is a real December fixture; 초대하다 takes the guests as 를
nuance: 파티 is a loanword from English 'party' and means a festive social gathering, usually private and fun (birthday, year-end, housewarming). Its trickiness is purely particle-based: take 에 to GO to one (파티에 가요) but 를 to HAVE/THROW one (파티를 해요/열어요), and use 에서 only when you name the location where the party happens (집에서 파티를 해요). The nearest rivals are 모임 and 잔치: 파티 is casual, Western-flavored, and fun-centered; 모임 is any get-together including serious ones (a book club is a 모임, not a 파티); 잔치 is a traditional Korean feast tied to a life milestone. Register is casual and youthful — you would not call a solemn ceremony a 파티. The main English-speaker pitfall is overusing 에서 with the motion verb 가다 (파티에서 가요 ✗): 에서 marks where something HAPPENS, so going TO the party needs 에. Also note Koreans rarely say 'party' for a simple dinner with friends — that is just a 모임 or a meal.

Using 만들다 to host (파티를 만들어요 ✗) — say 파티를 해요 or, more naturally, 파티를 열어요 'open/throw a party'.

usage: to attend / show up to a gathering
나가다 'go out (to)' is the idiomatic verb for joining a regular group meeting
to have a gathering (on the schedule)
이 marks 모임 as the thing that exists; 오늘 모임이 있어요
unlike 파티, 모임 CAN take 만들다 because you create the standing group itself
the qualifier (가족, 동창, 독서) tells you who gathers
examples: 오늘 모임이 있어요.
I have a gathering today.
simple: 있다 + 이 to state that a get-together is on the schedule
저는 한 달에 한 번 독서 모임에 나가요.
I attend a book club once a month.
everyday: 나가다 is the go-to verb for a recurring 모임; 독서 모임 = reading gathering
친구들과 작은 모임을 만들었어요.
I started a small group with my friends.
real-situation: here 모임 is the standing club you create, so 만들다 'make' is correct
nuance: 모임 is native Korean, built from the verb 모이다 'to gather/come together' plus the noun-forming -ㅁ, so it literally means 'a gathering.' It is the broadest, most neutral word for people coming together for a shared purpose — a club, a reunion, a regular dinner crew — and unlike 파티 it carries no festive or Western flavor. The sharp contrast: 파티 is fun and event-like; 회식 is specifically a work-team meal; 모임 is the umbrella term that can be any of these in a low-key way, including serious or hobby groups (독서 모임 'book club', 동창 모임 'alumni reunion'). Particle logic mirrors other event nouns: 에 to attend (모임에 가요/나가요) and 이 to say one exists (모임이 있어요). The English-speaker pitfall is again 에서 with 가다 (모임에서 가요 ✗) — use 에 for the destination. A subtler point: because 모임 can name the standing group, 모임을 만들다 'form a group' is fine, whereas the same phrase sounds odd with one-off 파티.

Forcing the English word 'party' onto every 모임 — a quiet hobby club or reunion is a 모임, not a 파티; choosing 파티 makes it sound like a festive event it isn't.
Using 하다 for joining (모임을 해요 to mean 'I attend') — to attend, use 모임에 나가다/가다; 모임을 하다 means the group itself meets/holds a session.

usage: to take part in an event
참여하다 'participate' fits the organized, formal tone of 행사 better than casual verbs
열리다 'be opened/held' is the standard passive for scheduled events; 가 marks the subject
진행하다 'proceed, conduct' is the organizer's verb (an MC 진행해요)
행사 takes a formal qualifier (기념, 개회, 졸업) signaling an official occasion
examples: 오늘 행사가 있어요.
There's an event today.
simple: 있다 + 가 to announce a scheduled official event
이번 주말에 회사에서 큰 행사를 해요.
The company is holding a big event this weekend.
everyday: 회사에서 (에서 = the organizer/place) + 행사를 (the object held)
많은 시민이 기념행사에 참여했습니다.
Many citizens took part in the commemorative event.
real-situation: formal 습니다 register; 참여하다 suits the official, public nature of a 행사
nuance: 행사 (行事, 行 'carry out/conduct' + 事 'affair/matter') is Sino-Korean and literally means 'a conducted affair' — i.e., an organized, often official or public event such as a ceremony, opening, campaign, or company function. Its tone is decidedly more formal and institutional than 파티 (fun, private) or 모임 (casual get-together): a corporate launch, a city festival's opening, a school sports day are all 행사. The near-synonym to separate from is 축제 'festival' — a 축제 is specifically a festive, celebratory event with crowds and entertainment, whereas 행사 is the neutral umbrella for any planned event, festive or solemn. Verbs run formal: 행사를 진행하다 'run an event', 행사가 열리다 'an event is held', 행사에 참여하다 'participate'. Particle pitfall as usual: 행사에 가요 for attending, never 행사에서 가요. English speakers also tend to reach for 'have a party' energy and pick casual verbs; with 행사, prefer 열다/진행하다/참여하다 to match its official register.

Using 행사 for a private fun party — that mismatches register; a birthday bash is a 파티, while 행사 implies an organized/official function.
Pairing it with overly casual verbs like 놀다 (행사를 놀아요 ✗) — say 행사에 참여하다 'take part' or 행사를 진행하다 'run it'.

usage: 에 marks the festival as your destination
즐기다 'enjoy, savor' is the typical experience verb; 를 marks the object
열리다 'be held' with 가; 봄마다 축제가 열려요
축제 commonly takes a place or season qualifier (부산, 벚꽃, 지역)
examples: 가을에 축제에 가요.
I go to a festival in autumn.
simple: 에 destination with the motion verb 가다
사람들이 거리에서 축제를 즐겨요.
People enjoy the festival in the streets.
everyday: 거리에서 (where it happens) + 축제를 즐기다 (enjoy as object)
매년 봄에 벚꽃 축제가 열려서 관광객이 많이 와요.
A cherry-blossom festival is held every spring, so many tourists come.
real-situation: 열리다 'be held' + the connector -어서 'so/because' linking cause and result
nuance: 축제 (祝祭, 祝 'celebrate/congratulate' + 祭 'rite/festival') is Sino-Korean, literally 'a celebratory rite,' and names a public festival full of food, music, performances and crowds — university festivals (대학 축제), cherry-blossom festivals, regional seasonal festivals. The key contrast is with 행사: 행사 is the neutral, possibly solemn umbrella for any organized event, while 축제 is specifically festive and joyful, so every 축제 is a kind of 행사 but not vice versa. Don't confuse it with 잔치 either — 잔치 is a private, traditional family feast (a baby's first birthday), whereas 축제 is large, public, and community-scale. Natural collocations: 축제가 열리다 'is held', 축제를 즐기다 'enjoy', 축제에 참가하다 'take part'. Register is neutral and warm. The recurring English-speaker pitfall is the particle: 축제에 가요 to attend, not 축제에서 가요 (에서 marks the spot where an action unfolds, e.g. 축제에서 공연을 봐요 'I watch a show AT the festival').

Using 축제 for a small private celebration — a family milestone party is a 잔치 or 파티; 축제 implies a large public event.
Pairing it with 보다 as the default verb (축제를 봐요) — you EXPERIENCE a festival, so 축제를 즐기다 'enjoy' or 축제에 가다 'go to' is more natural (you 보다 a specific 공연 inside it).

usage: you WATCH a show, so the verb is 보다 with 을, not 듣다
to give / put on a performance
the performer's side uses 하다: 가수가 공연을 해요
시작되다 'be started/begin' with 이; 곧 공연이 시작돼요
공연 + 시간 = the scheduled time or duration of the show
examples: 오늘 공연을 봐요.
I'm watching a show today.
simple: 보다 'watch' + 을, the core verb for a live show
그 가수가 무대에서 멋진 공연을 했어요.
That singer gave a great performance on stage.
everyday: 무대에서 (on stage, where it happens) + 공연을 하다 (the performer's verb)
공연이 곧 시작되니까 자리에 앉아 주세요.
The performance is about to start, so please take your seat.
real-situation: 시작되다 'begin' + -니까 'since/so' giving the reason for the request
nuance: 공연 (公演, 公 'public' + 演 'perform') is Sino-Korean, literally 'a public performance,' and covers live shows on a stage — concerts, plays, musicals, dance. The audience side uses 보다 'watch' (공연을 봐요) because it is something you see live; the performer side uses 하다 (공연을 해요). The near-synonym to separate is 콘서트 'concert,' which is narrower (a music gig), while 공연 is the broad cover term for any staged show; also distinguish 전시 'exhibition,' which you also 보다 but is static art you stroll past, not a timed live act. Useful collocations: 공연이 시작되다/끝나다 'the show starts/ends', 공연장 'performance venue'. Register is neutral. The big English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 듣다 'listen' because a concert is musical (공연을 들어요 ✗) — Korean treats the whole staged event as something you 보다 'watch', not 듣다; you only 듣다 the 음악/노래 inside it.

Mixing up audience and performer verbs — the viewer says 공연을 봐요, the artist says 공연을 해요; using 하다 about yourself wrongly claims you're performing.

usage: you VIEW it with your eyes, so 보다 + 를
열리다 'be held' with 가; 미술관에서 전시가 열려요
관람하다 'view (formally)' is the polite museum verb, more refined than 보다
전시 takes the content type as a qualifier (사진, 미술, 특별)
examples: 주말에 전시를 봐요.
I see an exhibition on the weekend.
simple: 보다 'see' + 를, the everyday verb for an exhibition
친구하고 미술관에서 사진 전시를 봤어요.
I saw a photo exhibition at the art museum with a friend.
everyday: 미술관에서 (where you view it) + 하고 'with' for the companion
이번 특별 전시는 관람료가 무료라서 사람이 많아요.
This special exhibition is free of charge, so it's crowded.
real-situation: 관람료 'viewing fee' + 무료 'free' + -라서 'because (it is)'
nuance: 전시 (展示, 展 'spread out/display' + 示 'show') is Sino-Korean, literally 'to spread out and show,' meaning a display of art, photos, or objects laid out for people to view. Because it is something you take in with your eyes, the verb is 보다 'see' (전시를 봐요) or the more formal 관람하다 'view'; the full event word is 전시회 (會 'meeting/gathering'), and the place is a 전시장 or 미술관. The sharp contrast is with 공연: both pair with 보다, but a 공연 is a timed live act you sit and watch start-to-finish, while a 전시 is a static collection you wander through at your own pace. Don't confuse it with 박람회 'expo/fair' either, which is a large commercial trade show. Register is neutral. The classic English-speaker pitfall is 듣다 'listen' (전시를 들어요 ✗) — there is nothing to listen to; you 보다 it. A second pitfall is saying 전시에 가요 thinking 전시 is a place; you go to the 전시회 or 미술관, and you 보다 the 전시.

The classic English-speaker pitfall is 듣다 'listen' (전시를 들어요 ✗) — there is nothing to listen to; you 보다 it. A second pitfall is saying 전시에 가요 thinking 전시 is a place; you go to the 전시회 or 미술관, and you 보다 the 전시.

Treating 전시 as a place you go to (전시에 가요) — go to the 전시회/미술관 and then 전시를 보다; 전시 names the display, not the venue.
Confusing 전시 with 공연 because both take 보다 — a 전시 is a static display you stroll through, a 공연 is a timed live act; pick by what you're actually watching.

usage: 데이트 needs 하다 to become an action; 를 marks it as the object
신청 'application/request' + 하다 = ask for a date; 데이트 신청을 받았어요 'I was asked out'
to go out on a date
-하러 가다 'go in order to do'; pairs the action with going somewhere
첫 'first' is the most common modifier; the milestone outing
examples: 주말에 데이트를 해요.
I'm going on a date this weekend.
simple: 데이트 + 하다 + 를, the basic 'go on a date' frame
남자친구하고 한강에서 데이트했어요.
I went on a date with my boyfriend at the Han River.
everyday: the partner takes 하고 'with', the spot takes 에서 'at'
어제 좋아하는 사람한테 데이트 신청을 했어요.
Yesterday I asked out the person I like.
real-situation: 한테 'to (a person)' + 데이트 신청을 하다 'ask out'
nuance: 데이트 is a loanword from English 'date' and means specifically a romantic outing between two people who are dating or interested in each other; like other loanword nouns it needs 하다 to act as a verb (데이트하다). The crucial boundary for English speakers is 데이트 vs 약속: English 'date' can mean a calendar appointment, but 데이트 is ONLY romantic — a business meeting or a plan to meet a friend is an 약속 (約束 'a binding promise'), never a 데이트. The partner is marked with 하고/와/과 'with' and the place with 에서; you do NOT mark the partner with 를. Natural collocations: 데이트 신청 'asking out', 첫 데이트 'first date', 소개팅 (a separate word for a blind date). Register is casual and youthful. The headline pitfall is exactly the false friend: do not say 'I have a date with my client' as 손님하고 데이트가 있어요 — that implies romance; use 약속/미팅 instead.

usage: to go to the team dinner
에 marks the company dinner as your destination
이 marks 회식 as the thing that exists; 오늘 회식이 있어요
the team's action verb is 하다; 팀이 회식을 해요
자리 'seat/occasion' = the social setting of the dinner (회식 자리에서 'at the team dinner')
examples: 오늘 회식이 있어요.
There's a company dinner today.
simple: 있다 + 이 to announce a scheduled work dinner
퇴근 후에 팀 회식에 가요.
After work I'm going to the team dinner.
everyday: 퇴근 후에 'after leaving work' + 회식에 가다 (destination 에)
요즘은 회식을 강요하지 않는 회사가 많아졌어요.
These days more companies don't force employees to attend team dinners.
real-situation: 강요하다 'force' + 많아지다 'become many' — reflects real workplace-culture change
nuance: 회식 (會食, 會 'gather/meet' + 食 'eat') is Sino-Korean, literally 'a gathering to eat,' and means a meal that coworkers share together as a team, usually after work and often with drinks — a defining feature of Korean company culture. The contrast to nail is 회식 vs 모임: a 회식 is specifically a work/organization meal you attend as part of your job, with an implicit hierarchy (your 부장 'department head' is there), whereas a 모임 is any casual social gathering by choice. It is also not a 파티 — a 회식 centers on eating and bonding under workplace norms, not festive celebration. Common collocations: 부서 회식 'department dinner', 회식 자리 'the dinner setting', 1차/2차 (the 'first/second round' of venues a 회식 moves through). Register is neutral but the concept itself is loaded with social obligation. The English-speaker pitfall is the usual particle slip (회식에서 가요 ✗ → 회식에 가요) and assuming it is optional fun; culturally it can carry expectation, though that is changing.

usage: 에 marks the feast as your destination
벌이다 'spread out, throw' is the vivid traditional verb for staging a big feast
열리다 'be held' with 가; 마을에 잔치가 열려요
fixed compound: 돌 'first birthday' + 잔치; a major Korean family celebration
examples: 오늘 잔치에 가요.
I'm going to a feast today.
simple: 에 destination with 가다
할머니 생신에 가족들이 모여 잔치를 했어요.
On Grandma's birthday the family gathered and held a feast.
everyday: 생신 (honorific 'birthday') + 모이다 'gather' + 잔치를 하다
조카 돌잔치에 가서 축하해 줬어요.
I went to my nephew's first-birthday feast and congratulated him.
real-situation: 돌잔치 as a fixed word + -아 주다 'do (for someone)'
nuance: 잔치 is a native Korean word for a traditional feast — a celebratory gathering with plenty of food and invited guests to mark a life milestone (a baby's 돌잔치 'first birthday', a 60th birthday 환갑잔치, a wedding feast). Its flavor is warm, communal, and culturally Korean, distinct from the loanword 파티 (modern, Western, fun-centered) and from 회식 (a work meal). The sharpest contrast is 잔치 vs 축제: a 잔치 is private and family/community-based around a personal milestone, while a 축제 is a large public festival open to strangers. Note the idiom 잔치국수 'banquet noodles', the simple noodle dish historically served at feasts (especially weddings). Verbs lean traditional: 잔치를 벌이다/하다 'throw a feast', 잔치가 열리다 'is held'. Register is neutral and homey. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle (잔치에서 가요 ✗ → 잔치에 가요) and over-reaching for 파티 — calling a grandparent's milestone feast a 파티 misses the traditional, family-honoring tone that 잔치 carries.

usage: 받다 'receive' is the invitee's verb; 결혼식 초대를 받았어요
the host's verb; the guest takes 를 and the place takes 에: 친구를 집에 초대해요
응하다 'comply/respond to' takes 에; the formal way to say you accept
초대 + 장 (狀 'document') = the physical invitation; 청첩장 is specifically a wedding one
examples: 초대해 줘서 고마워요.
Thank you for inviting me.
simple: 초대하다 + -아 주다 'do for me' + 고마워요 — a set thank-you for being invited
친구가 저를 생일 파티에 초대했어요.
My friend invited me to a birthday party.
everyday: guest = 저를 (object 를), event = 파티에 (에) — the standard invite frame
결혼식 초대를 받았는데 그날 못 갈 것 같아요.
I got a wedding invitation, but I probably can't make it that day.
real-situation: 초대를 받다 'receive an invite' + -는데 'but/and' setting up the contrast
nuance: 초대 (招待, 招 'beckon/summon' + 待 'treat/host') is Sino-Korean, literally 'to beckon and host,' and means an invitation to an event or one's home, with the implication of hosting the guest warmly. It splits cleanly by viewpoint: the host 초대를 하다/초대하다 'gives/extends' an invitation (guest = 를, place = 에), and the guest 초대를 받다 'receives' one. The near-synonym to separate is 부르다 'to call (someone over)' — 부르다 is casual and direct ('I called my friends over'), while 초대하다 is more formal and implies a proper, hosted occasion. Don't confuse 초대장 'invitation card' with 청첩장, which is specifically a wedding invitation. Register is neutral-polite. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 초대 like a thing you 'go' to (초대를 가요 ✗) — you don't go to an invitation; you 받다 'receive' it, then go to the EVENT. Another slip is dropping the directional logic: the person invited is the object (저를 초대했어요), not the destination.

usage: 참석하다 'attend (formally)' suits a ceremony better than plain 가다; takes 에
이 marks the ceremony as the thing that exists; 내일 졸업식이 있어요
열리다 'be held' with 이; 강당에서 졸업식이 열려요
졸업식 + 사진; the keepsake photo taken at the ceremony
examples: 내일 졸업식에 가요.
I'm going to a graduation tomorrow.
simple: 에 destination with 가다
다음 주에 동생 졸업식에 참석할 거예요.
Next week I'll attend my younger sibling's graduation.
everyday: 참석하다 'attend' + -ㄹ 거예요 'will' for a planned future
졸업식이 끝나고 가족들과 사진을 많이 찍었어요.
After the graduation, I took lots of photos with my family.
real-situation: -고 'and then' sequencing + 사진을 찍다 'take photos'
nuance: 졸업식 (卒業式) breaks down as 졸업 (卒 'finish' + 業 'studies/work') 'graduation' plus 식 (式 'ceremony/rite'), so it literally means 'finishing-studies ceremony' — the formal event held when students complete a school. Keep the two pieces straight: 졸업 is the act/fact of graduating (졸업했어요 'I graduated'), while 졸업식 is the ceremony you attend (졸업식에 가요); the antonym ceremony for starting school is 입학식 (入學式 'entering-school ceremony'). The 식 'ceremony' suffix is highly productive — 결혼식 'wedding', 입학식, 장례식 'funeral', 개회식 'opening ceremony' — so learning it unlocks a whole family of event words. Verbs are formal: 졸업식에 참석하다 'attend', 졸업식이 열리다 'is held'. Register is neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle (졸업식에서 가요 ✗ → 졸업식에 가요), and confusing 졸업 with 졸업식 — say 졸업했어요 for 'I graduated', but 졸업식에 갔어요 for 'I went to the graduation ceremony.'
